  • CTRL-0096 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Harden agent frameworks and runtimes before exposing them, and patch framework vulnerabilities promptly

Sources: https://www.reco.ai/blog/openclaw-the-ai-agent-security-crisis-unfolding-right-now · https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/langgraph-flaw-chain-exposes-self.html · https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/05/prompt-injection-isnt-the-bug-ai-agent-frameworks-are/5283585

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI03, ASI05; OWASP threat T3, T11

docs.title: Design: Monitoring and Traceability (DSN-03)
docs.text: Monitoring and traceability provide systematic visibility into agent behaviour, interactions, and decision pathways by recording, observing, and correlating agent actions and system events over time. This includes logging agent inputs and outputs, tracking tool invocations and state changes, capturing decision traces or execution paths, and surfacing telemetry or audit records that support analysis and review of system behaviour.

docs.title: RISK-017 · Delayed failure detection due to limited monitoring
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Monitoring and Traceability (DSN-03) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when monitoring systems provide insufficient visibility into agent behaviour, system events, or execution outcomes. As a result, failures, anomalies, or unintended actions may go undetected for extended periods, increasing the impact and difficulty of remediation.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0032 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Centralise observability data collection in a unified backend system
  • CTRL-0033 (Level 1 · Standard): Standardise trace attributes for agent operations using consistent semantic conventions

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13138

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI08; OWASP threat T8

docs.title: RISK-018 · Inability to audit failures due to missing decision traces
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Monitoring and Traceability (DSN-03) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02)

This risk arises when monitoring systems do not capture sufficient reasoning steps, decision pathways, or execution context for agent actions. As a result, operators may be unable to reconstruct failures, understand why specific outcomes occurred, or conduct effective audits and post-incident reviews.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0032 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Centralise observability data collection in a unified backend system
  • CTRL-0034 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Conduct regular reviews of logs and traces to detect emergent issues in deployed agentic systems

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05285 · https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI08, ASI10; OWASP threat T8

docs.title: RISK-052 · Automation bias and erosion of human oversight
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Monitoring and Traceability (DSN-03) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when human approval steps stop providing meaningful review: overseers approve by default under volume (one large deployment measured users approving around 93% of permission prompts), lack the context or expertise to evaluate what the agent proposes, or use interfaces designed for speed rather than scrutiny. Controls that assume a considered human decision then give false assurance, and adversaries can exploit the trust users place in fluent, confident agents. As a result, high-impact actions proceed with nominal rather than actual oversight.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0006 (Level 1 · Standard): Require human approval before executing high-impact actions
  • CTRL-0042 (Level 1 · Standard): Require explicit human confirmation before executing high-impact or irreversible tool actions
  • CTRL-0049 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement UI/UX cues to communicate the risk of hallucination to users
  • CTRL-0094 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps

Sources: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude · https://www.imda.gov.sg/-/media/imda/files/about/emerging-tech-and-research/artificial-intelligence/mgf-for-agentic-ai.pdf · https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI09; OWASP threat T10

docs.title: Capability: Planning and Goal Management (CAP-01)
docs.text: The capability to develop detailed, step-by-step, and executable plans with specific tasks in response to broad instructions. This includes prioritizing activities based on importance and dependencies between tasks, monitoring how well its plan is working, and adjusting when circumstances change or obstacles arise.

docs.title: RISK-019 · Generating plans that fail to meet the user's requirements
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Planning and Goal Management (CAP-01) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent generates plans or goals that do not accurately reflect the user’s stated objectives, constraints, or preferences. As a result, the system may pursue incorrect or suboptimal actions, waste resources, or deliver outcomes that do not satisfy user expectations.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0006 (Level 1 · Standard): Require human approval before executing high-impact actions
  • CTRL-0035 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Require agents to decompose user goals into explicit sub-goals and validate necessity before proceeding
  • CTRL-0036 (Level 1 · Standard): Regularly evaluate and test planning behaviour under representative workloads and failure scenarios

Sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.01622v4 · https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.93.pdf

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01; OWASP threat T6

docs.title: RISK-020 · Generating plans that overlook safety implications
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Planning and Goal Management (CAP-01) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent generates plans or goals without adequately considering basic safety, security, or practical constraints that would be apparent to a human. As a result, the system may propose or pursue actions that are unsafe, insecure, or inappropriate despite being technically feasible.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0006 (Level 1 · Standard): Require human approval before executing high-impact actions
  • CTRL-0035 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Require agents to decompose user goals into explicit sub-goals and validate necessity before proceeding
  • CTRL-0037 (Level 1 · Standard): Require planning agents to include explicit safety constraints in all generated plans before execution
  • CTRL-0038 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Conduct safety verification with domain-relevant stress tests and adversarial scenarios before deployment and on a regular cadence afterwards
  • CTRL-0039 (Level 1 · Standard): Ensure each agent publishes standardised, machine-readable capability descriptors accessible to other agents

Sources: https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/ai-still-lacks-common-sense-70-years

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI10, ASI01; OWASP threat T7

docs.title: Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02)
docs.text: The capability to assign subtasks to other agents and coordinate their activities to achieve broader goals. This includes identifying which components are best suited for specific tasks, issuing clear instructions, managing inter-agent dependencies, and monitoring performance or failures. A system has this capability whenever more than one agent works on a task, whether an agent decides the hand-offs or they are fixed in the workflow, and whether the other agents belong to the same system or are operated by another party, including agents it transacts with as counterparties.

docs.title: RISK-021 · Incorrect task delegation between agents
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Identity and access management (HZ-04), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent assigns tasks to other agents that do not match their capabilities, roles, or access permissions. As a result, tasks may be executed incorrectly, fail to complete, or introduce security and operational issues due to inappropriate delegation.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0040 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Limit the scope of agent actions through predefined thresholds and baselines

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI03, ASI08; OWASP threat T3

docs.title: RISK-022 · Malicious or manipulative use of delegated agents
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Identity and access management (HZ-04), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent deliberately assigns tasks to other agents in ways intended to bypass controls, obscure responsibility, or achieve malicious objectives. As a result, delegated agents may be coerced into performing unauthorised actions, amplifying harmful behaviour or evading detection within the system.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0008 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement automated alerts when agent behaviour drifts from predefined thresholds
  • CTRL-0024 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
  • CTRL-0025 (Level 1 · Standard): Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
  • CTRL-0041 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Provide comprehensive descriptions for each tool including intended use, required inputs, and potential outputs
  • CTRL-0093 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Monitor agents for deceptive and collusive behaviour using an independent monitor

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06850

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI10, ASI03; OWASP threat T13, T14

docs.title: RISK-053 · Dependence on third-party agents as counterparties or delegates
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: Tool or Resource Malfunction · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when tasks are delegated to, or transactions conducted with, agents provided or operated by external parties — SaaS agents, partner agents reached through protocols such as A2A — whose instructions, tools, data handling, and updates are outside the organisation's control. Delegated work may be performed unsafely, data shared with the agent may be retained or reused, and behaviour can change without notice. As a result, the organisation carries the consequences of failures it cannot observe or govern directly.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0024 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
  • CTRL-0025 (Level 1 · Standard): Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
  • CTRL-0026 (Level 1 · Standard): Require all agents to authenticate with verifiable, cryptographically signed identities before processing requests
  • CTRL-0039 (Level 1 · Standard): Ensure each agent publishes standardised, machine-readable capability descriptors accessible to other agents
  • CTRL-0040 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Limit the scope of agent actions through predefined thresholds and baselines
  • CTRL-0095 (Level 1 · Standard): Apply due diligence and technical bounds to third-party agents before delegating to them or transacting with them

Sources: https://www.imda.gov.sg/-/media/imda/files/about/emerging-tech-and-research/artificial-intelligence/mgf-for-agentic-ai.pdf · https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/a2a-protocol-surpasses-150-organizations-lands-in-major-cloud-platforms-and-sees-enterprise-production-use-in-first-year · https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI04, ASI07; OWASP threat T13

docs.title: Capability: Tool Use (CAP-03)
docs.text: The capability to evaluate available options and choose the best tool for specific subtasks, based on the capabilities and limitations of different tools and matching them appropriately to the tasks. This includes selecting between search, computation, code execution, or domain-specific APIs, determining when tool invocation is necessary, and sequencing or combining multiple tools to complete complex tasks effectively.

docs.title: RISK-023 · Incorrect tool selection or misuse
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Tool Use (CAP-03) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent selects an inappropriate tool or applies a tool incorrectly for a given task or action. As a result, the agent may produce erroneous outcomes, fail to complete the task effectively, or trigger unintended side effects due to misuse of tool capabilities.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0041 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Provide comprehensive descriptions for each tool including intended use, required inputs, and potential outputs
  • CTRL-0042 (Level 1 · Standard): Require explicit human confirmation before executing high-impact or irreversible tool actions
  • CTRL-0043 (Level 1 · Standard): Log all tool selection decisions and invocations with comprehensive metadata

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13547

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T2

docs.title: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04)
docs.text: The capability to communicate with human users across multiple modalities, including natural language conversation (explaining topics, generating documents, interactive discussions) and multimodal understanding/generation (processing and creating image, audio, or video content such as visual analysis, speech transcription, or multimedia creation).

docs.title: RISK-024 · Generation of undesirable content
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Discriminatory or hateful content (HZ-06), Inappropriate content (HZ-07)

This risk arises when an agent generates text, images, audio, or other media that contain toxic, hateful, sexual, or otherwise inappropriate content. As a result, the system may cause harm to users, violate organisational standards or regulations, or undermine trust in the system’s outputs.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0044 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement output safety guardrails to detect and prevent generation of undesirable content

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04249v2

docs.title: RISK-025 · Generation of unqualified advice in specialised domains
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent generates advice or guidance in specialised domains such as medical, financial, or legal contexts without appropriate expertise, validation, or safeguards. As a result, users may act on incorrect or inappropriate information, leading to potential harm or adverse outcomes.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0045 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement input guardrails to detect and decline requests for specialised domain advice

Sources: https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-04/ai-privacy-risks-and-mitigations-in-llms.pdf

docs.title: RISK-026 · Generation of controversial or sensitive content
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Inappropriate content (HZ-07), Misrepresentation (HZ-09)

This risk arises when an agent generates content related to sensitive or controversial topics, such as political commentary or denigrating comments about competitors. As a result, the system may create reputational, legal, or compliance issues, or be perceived as biased, inappropriate, or misrepresentative of organisational views.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0046 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement input guardrails to detect and decline requests for controversial content that violates organisational policies

Sources: https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2025/05/ai-models-llms-chatgpt-claude-gemini-partisan-bias-research-study

docs.title: RISK-027 · Regurgitating personally identifiable information
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent reproduces personally identifiable information in its generated outputs, whether drawn from training data, memory, or prior interactions. As a result, the system may violate privacy obligations, expose individuals to harm, or breach data protection requirements.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0047 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement output guardrails to detect and redact personally identifiable information

Sources: https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-04/ai-privacy-risks-and-mitigations-in-llms.pdf

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI06; OWASP threat T1

docs.title: RISK-028 · Generation of non-factual or hallucinated content
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Compromised user safety (HZ-08), Misrepresentation (HZ-09)

This risk arises when an agent generates information that is inaccurate, fabricated, or unsupported by evidence while presenting it as factual. As a result, users may be misled, make incorrect decisions, or lose trust in the system’s outputs.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0048 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Implement methods to reduce hallucination rates in agent outputs
  • CTRL-0049 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement UI/UX cues to communicate the risk of hallucination to users
  • CTRL-0050 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement features enabling users to verify generated answers against source content

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.01219

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI08; OWASP threat T5

docs.title: RISK-029 · Generation of copyrighted content
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Multimodal Understanding and Generation (CAP-04) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Illegal and CBRNE activities (HZ-05)

This risk arises when an agent generates content that reproduces or closely resembles copyrighted material without appropriate rights or attribution. As a result, the system may infringe intellectual property laws, expose the organisation to legal liability, or violate licensing and usage terms.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0051 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement input guardrails to detect and decline requests to generate copyrighted content

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07087

docs.title: Capability: Official Communication (CAP-05)
docs.text: The capability to autonomously compose, finalize, and dispatch authoritative communications that formally and legally represent an organization to external parties (e.g. customers, partners, regulators, courts, or media) via approved channels and formats, without prior human review or approval, thereby creating potential legal, regulatory, or reputational obligations. This includes sending legally binding correspondence, publishing official statements or press releases, and responding to external inquiries using the organisation's identity.

docs.title: RISK-030 · Misrepresentation of authorship
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Official Communication (CAP-05) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Misrepresentation (HZ-09)

This risk arises when recipients are misled about whether an official communication was authored by a human or generated by an agent on behalf of the organisation. As a result, stakeholders may form incorrect assumptions about accountability, intent, or authority, potentially leading to trust, legal, or reputational issues.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0052 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Declare upfront that communications are generated by an AI system

Sources: https://fortune.com/article/customer-support-ai-cursor-went-rogue/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI09; OWASP threat T15

docs.title: RISK-031 · Inaccurate promises or statements in official communications
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Official Communication (CAP-05) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety · Hazards: Misrepresentation (HZ-09)

This risk arises when an agent makes commitments, assurances, or public statements that are incorrect, unsupported, or exceed the organisation’s actual intentions or capabilities. As a result, the organisation may face reputational damage, legal exposure, or loss of public trust due to unmet expectations or misinformation.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0053 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Require human approval for communications on sensitive matters
  • CTRL-0054 (Level 1 · Standard): Limit agent communications to standard processes with predefined templates
  • CTRL-0055 (Level 1 · Standard): Provide alternative channels for users to clarify communications or provide feedback
  • CTRL-0094 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps

Sources: https://the-decoder.com/people-buy-brand-new-chevrolets-for-1-from-a-chatgpt-chatbot/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI09; OWASP threat T15

docs.title: Capability: Business Transactions (CAP-06)
docs.text: The capability to autonomously initiate, authorise, and execute binding business transactions with external parties - such as payments, purchases, reservations, or service commitments - within predefined authorisation limits, resulting in real financial, contractual, or operational obligations for the organization. This includes processing payments or refunds, placing orders or subscriptions, booking services or reservations, and accepting or triggering contractual commitments on behalf of the organization.

docs.title: RISK-032 · Unauthorised execution of business transactions
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Business Transactions (CAP-06) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Identity and access management (HZ-04)

This risk arises when an agent initiates, authorises, or executes business transactions outside predefined approval thresholds, roles, or authorisation limits. As a result, the organisation may be exposed to unintended financial losses, binding contractual obligations, or operational commitments that were not properly sanctioned.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0056 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Require explicit human confirmation before committing any business transaction outside limits that an accountable human has pre-authorised
  • CTRL-0057 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Require out-of-band confirmation when transaction risk signals are elevated
  • CTRL-0058 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Restrict agents to proposing transactions whilst using a separate transaction controller for execution
  • CTRL-0059 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Apply fraud detection models or heuristics to agent-proposed transactions
  • CTRL-0094 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps

Sources: https://www.emergingtechbrew.com/stories/2025/05/29/ai-agents-vulnerable-financial-attacks

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02, ASI01; OWASP threat T2, T6

docs.title: RISK-033 · Leakage of transaction credentials
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Business Transactions (CAP-06) Failure mode: Tool or Resource Malfunction · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Identity and access management (HZ-04)

This risk arises when credentials, tokens, or sensitive authentication information used to execute business transactions are exposed, mishandled, or improperly stored by an agent or its supporting systems. As a result, malicious parties may gain the ability to initiate unauthorised transactions, manipulate financial operations, or compromise transactional systems.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0058 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Restrict agents to proposing transactions whilst using a separate transaction controller for execution

Sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01055

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI03; OWASP threat T3

docs.title: Capability: Internet and Search Access (CAP-07)
docs.text: The capability to autonomously access, browse, search, and retrieve information from the Internet to augment the LLM's static training knowledge with external and up-to-date sources in support of task execution and response generation. This includes issuing search queries, following and parsing web pages, extracting relevant facts or documents, and aggregating information from multiple online sources.

docs.title: RISK-034 · Prompt injection via malicious websites
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Internet and Search Access (CAP-07) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent retrieves or processes content from malicious or untrusted websites that are designed to inject instructions or manipulative prompts into the system. As a result, the agent may follow unintended commands, override intended constraints, or take actions that compromise system behaviour or integrity.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0060 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement escape filtering before incorporating web content into prompts
  • CTRL-0061 (Level 1 · Standard): Use structured retrieval APIs for web searches rather than web scraping
  • CTRL-0062 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement input guardrails to detect prompt injection and adversarial attacks
  • CTRL-0090 (Level 1 · Standard): Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions

Sources: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agentic-ai-threats/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01; OWASP threat T6

docs.title: RISK-035 · Unreliable information or websites
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Internet and Search Access (CAP-07) Failure mode: Tool or Resource Malfunction · Type: Safety · Hazards: Compromised user safety (HZ-08), Misrepresentation (HZ-09)

This risk arises when an agent retrieves and presents information from websites that are inaccurate, outdated, biased, or otherwise unreliable. As a result, users may be misinformed or make incorrect decisions based on content that has not been adequately validated or corroborated.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0063 (Level 1 · Standard): Prioritise search results from verified, high-quality domains

Sources: https://www.techradar.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/googles-ai-overviews-are-often-so-confidently-wrong-that-ive-lost-all-trust-in-them

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI06; OWASP threat T5

docs.title: Capability: Computer Use (CAP-08)
docs.text: The capability to directly operate a computer’s graphical user interface on behalf of the user, enabling the agent to navigate applications and execute tasks through mouse, keyboard, and window-based interactions. This includes moving the cursor, clicking buttons, entering text, using keyboard shortcuts, switching between windows and applications, and navigating files and menus within the operating system environment.

docs.title: RISK-036 · Prompt injection risks through computer use
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Computer Use (CAP-08) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent interacts with graphical user interfaces that display untrusted or adversarial content - such as web pages, documents, pop-ups, or form fields - crafted to embed hidden instructions or manipulative cues. As a result, the agent may misinterpret on-screen text as authoritative guidance, follow injected instructions, or perform unintended actions while operating the interface.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0062 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement input guardrails to detect prompt injection and adversarial attacks
  • CTRL-0064 (Level 1 · Standard): Limit computer use to accessing only safe and trusted resources
  • CTRL-0065 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Ensure every agent can be immediately paused or terminated by its operators
  • CTRL-0090 (Level 1 · Standard): Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions

Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.13076v1 · https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/indirect-prompt-injection-of-claude-computer-use/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01; OWASP threat T6

docs.title: RISK-037 · Exposure of sensitive data
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Computer Use (CAP-08) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent operating a computer interface accesses websites or applications that contain personally identifiable or sensitive information, particularly when authenticated as a user or organisation. As a result, the agent may inadvertently view, process, or disclose confidential data beyond its intended scope or authorisation.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0047 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement output guardrails to detect and redact personally identifiable information
  • CTRL-0066 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Ensure "take over" mode is activated when entering sensitive data
  • CTRL-0089 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enforce default-deny network egress for agent runtimes, allowing only approved destinations
  • CTRL-0097 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent

Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.00618v3

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T2

docs.title: Capability: Other Programmatic Interfaces (CAP-09)
docs.text: The capability to interact with external systems through non-graphical, programmatic interfaces, such as APIs, SDKs, and backend services, to exchange data or trigger actions as part of task execution. This includes calling REST or GraphQL APIs, invoking cloud services, publishing or consuming messages from queues or event streams, and performing operations such as code pushes, data updates, or system integrations across enterprise platforms. This includes sending and receiving email, chat, or other messages through an API or mail protocol, including when those messages are also Official Communication (CAP-05).

docs.title: RISK-038 · Incorrect use of unfamiliar programmatic interfaces
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Other Programmatic Interfaces (CAP-09) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent interacts with programmatic interfaces it has not been trained or configured to use correctly, particularly bespoke or non-standard interfaces outside established protocols such as MCP servers. As a result, the agent may misinterpret interface semantics, invoke operations incorrectly, or produce unintended effects due to improper integration or usage.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0041 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Provide comprehensive descriptions for each tool including intended use, required inputs, and potential outputs
  • CTRL-0067 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Ensure proper documentation of programmatic interfaces for agent use

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15817

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T2

docs.title: Capability: Code Execution (CAP-10)
docs.text: The capability to write, execute, and debug code in various programming languages to automate tasks or solve computational problems. This includes implementing algorithms, writing scripts, compiling and running code, debugging errors, and integrating with external systems through APIs or backend services.

docs.title: RISK-039 · Production or execution of poor or ineffective code
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Code Execution (CAP-10) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02)

This risk arises when an agent generates or executes code that is incorrect, inefficient, insecure, or unsuitable for the intended task. As a result, the code may fail to achieve desired outcomes, introduce bugs or vulnerabilities, or cause operational disruptions when deployed or run.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0068 (Level 1 · Standard): Use code linters to screen generated code for bad practices and poor syntax
  • CTRL-0069 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Run agent-generated code only in isolated compute environments with network access blocked by default
  • CTRL-0070 (Level 1 · Standard): Review all agent-generated code before execution
  • CTRL-0071 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Use static code analysers to detect security vulnerabilities and code quality issues
  • CTRL-0072 (Level 1 · Standard): Monitor runtime and memory consumption of agent-generated code

Sources: https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity25/sec25cycle1-prepub-742-spracklen.pdf · https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ · https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/bfd082c452dffb450d5a5202b0419205-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI05; OWASP threat T11

docs.title: RISK-040 · Production or execution of vulnerable or malicious code
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Code Execution (CAP-10) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Application (HZ-02)

This risk arises when an agent executes code that contains security vulnerabilities or intentionally malicious logic, whether generated by the model or sourced externally. As a result, the system may be compromised through exploitation, unauthorised access, data leakage, or other harmful effects.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0069 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Run agent-generated code only in isolated compute environments with network access blocked by default
  • CTRL-0070 (Level 1 · Standard): Review all agent-generated code before execution
  • CTRL-0071 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Use static code analysers to detect security vulnerabilities and code quality issues
  • CTRL-0072 (Level 1 · Standard): Monitor runtime and memory consumption of agent-generated code
  • CTRL-0073 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Create a denylist of commands that agents are not permitted to execute
  • CTRL-0074 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Conduct CVE scanning and block execution of code with High or Critical vulnerabilities

Sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.08200 · https://arxiv.org/html/2504.21205v1

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI05; OWASP threat T11

docs.title: Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11)
docs.text: The capability to manage the full lifecycle of files and data by creating, reading, modifying, organizing, converting, querying, and updating information across both unstructured artifacts (e.g. documents, spreadsheets, media files) and structured data stores (e.g. SQL/NoSQL databases, data warehouses, vector or embedding stores) in support of operational tasks. This includes ingesting and transforming datasets, generating or updating files, maintaining directory or schema structures, executing database queries or updates, and storing or retrieving embeddings or derived data products.

docs.title: RISK-041 · Unintended overwriting or deletion of files or data
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01)

This risk arises when an agent modifies, overwrites, or deletes files, database tables, or datasets without explicit user instruction or authorisation. As a result, critical information may be lost or corrupted, leading to data integrity issues, operational disruption, or the need for costly recovery efforts.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0075 (Level 1 · Standard): Do not grant write access to agents unless strictly necessary
  • CTRL-0076 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Require human approval for destructive changes to databases, tables, or files that cannot be readily undone
  • CTRL-0077 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enable versioning or soft-delete for managed object stores to allow recovery from accidental modifications
  • CTRL-0094 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps

Sources: https://syssec.dpss.inesc-id.pt/papers/pedro_icse25.pdf

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T2

docs.title: RISK-042 · Database overload due to inefficient data operations
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Infrastructure and network (HZ-03)

This risk arises when an agent issues poorly optimised, excessively frequent, or redundant queries against databases or data stores. As a result, system performance may degrade, resources may be exhausted, or critical services may become unavailable due to unnecessary load.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0078 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enforce throttling or rate limits on agent-initiated database operations
  • CTRL-0079 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Validate agent-generated database queries for efficiency before execution against production databases
  • CTRL-0080 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Implement caching mechanisms to reduce repetitive database queries by agents

Sources: https://www.tinybird.co/blog-posts/which-llm-writes-the-best-sql

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T4

docs.title: RISK-043 · Exposure of sensitive data through file or database access
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01)

This risk arises when an agent accesses, processes, or outputs personally identifiable or sensitive information stored in files or databases without appropriate safeguards. As a result, confidential data may be disclosed to unauthorised parties, leading to privacy breaches, regulatory non-compliance, or loss of trust.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0047 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement output guardrails to detect and redact personally identifiable information
  • CTRL-0081 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement input guardrails to detect personally identifiable information in data accessed by agents
  • CTRL-0082 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Do not grant agents access to personally identifiable or sensitive data unless strictly required

Sources: https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/microsoft-365-copilot-zeroclick-ai/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02, ASI03; OWASP threat T2, T3

docs.title: RISK-044 · Prompt injection via malicious files or data
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent ingests or processes maliciously crafted files or data that embed hidden instructions or manipulative content. As a result, the agent may follow unintended prompts, alter its behaviour, or execute actions that compromise system safety or integrity.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0062 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement input guardrails to detect prompt injection and adversarial attacks
  • CTRL-0083 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Disallow unknown or external files unless they have been scanned for threats
  • CTRL-0090 (Level 1 · Standard): Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
  • CTRL-0097 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent

Sources: https://www.hackthebox.com/blog/cve-2025-32711-echoleak-copilot-vulnerability · https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01, ASI06; OWASP threat T6, T1

docs.title: Capability: System Management (CAP-12)
docs.text: The capability to directly manage and configure technical systems and infrastructure by adjusting system settings, controlling computing resources, and administering operational environments across on-premise or cloud platforms. This includes monitoring system health and performance, managing authentication credentials and access controls, provisioning or scaling compute and storage resources, configuring operating system or runtime parameters, and applying system-level optimisations to support reliable operation.

docs.title: RISK-045 · Misconfiguration of system resources
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: System Management (CAP-12) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Infrastructure and network (HZ-03)

This risk arises when an agent incorrectly configures system settings, infrastructure resources, or operational parameters. As a result, system performance, reliability, or security may be degraded, leading to service disruptions or unintended operational behaviour.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0084 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Set minimum and maximum limits on what agents can modify within system resources
  • CTRL-0085 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Log system health metrics and implement automated alerts for abnormal conditions

Sources: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/97835 · https://arxiv.org/html/2507.10584v1

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02, ASI08; OWASP threat T2

docs.title: RISK-046 · System overload due to inefficient or excessive operations
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: System Management (CAP-12) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Security · Hazards: Infrastructure and network (HZ-03)

This risk arises when an agent issues poorly optimised, excessively frequent, or redundant system-level operations or queries. As a result, computing resources may be exhausted, system performance may degrade, or services may become unavailable due to unnecessary load.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0086 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Limit the number of concurrent queries to external systems by agents

Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20859v1 · https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm102025-unbounded-consumption/

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI02; OWASP threat T4

docs.title: RISK-012 · Cascading errors in multi-agent architectures
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Agentic Architecture (DSN-01) + Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Application (HZ-02), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when errors or misjudgements produced by one agent propagate through interconnected agents within a multi-agent system. As a result, small failures may compound across agent interactions, leading to amplified errors, degraded system performance, or unintended outcomes at the system level.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0024 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
  • CTRL-0025 (Level 1 · Standard): Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
  • CTRL-0027 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures in multi-agent systems
  • CTRL-0028 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Continuously monitor multi-agent systems for cascade failure indicators

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00989v3 · https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.19145

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI08; OWASP threat T5

docs.title: RISK-013 · Man-in-the-middle attacks between agents
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Agentic Architecture (DSN-01) + Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01), Infrastructure and network (HZ-03)

This risk arises when communication channels between agents are insufficiently secured, allowing an attacker to intercept, modify, or replay messages exchanged within the agentic system. As a result, agents may act on tampered information, leading to incorrect coordination, unauthorised actions, or compromised system behaviour.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0026 (Level 1 · Standard): Require all agents to authenticate with verifiable, cryptographically signed identities before processing requests
  • CTRL-0027 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures in multi-agent systems

Sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.14847

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI07; OWASP threat T12, T9

docs.title: RISK-047 · Data exfiltration through combined access to untrusted content, sensitive data, and an outbound channel
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Internet and Search Access (CAP-07) + Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01)

This risk arises when an agent that ingests untrusted content (web pages, files, messages) also holds access to sensitive data and has any outbound channel — browsing itself, API calls, messaging, or tool calls that carry data in URLs — so that instructions injected through the retrieval path can direct the agent to send data out through a legitimate tool. Each capability may be individually controlled; the exposure comes from their combination. As a result, confidential data can leave the organisation without any single control being bypassed, as demonstrated by ForcedLeak and EchoLeak. RISK-055 covers the same combination when the untrusted content arrives through messages or APIs rather than the web.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0020 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Use a dedicated LLM to extract required fields from inputs and filter out extraneous text or embedded instructions
  • CTRL-0060 (Level 1 · Standard): Implement escape filtering before incorporating web content into prompts
  • CTRL-0062 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement input guardrails to detect prompt injection and adversarial attacks
  • CTRL-0082 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Do not grant agents access to personally identifiable or sensitive data unless strictly required
  • CTRL-0083 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Disallow unknown or external files unless they have been scanned for threats
  • CTRL-0089 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enforce default-deny network egress for agent runtimes, allowing only approved destinations
  • CTRL-0090 (Level 1 · Standard): Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
  • CTRL-0097 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent

Sources: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ · https://www.varonis.com/blog/forcedleak · https://www.hackthebox.com/blog/cve-2025-32711-echoleak-copilot-vulnerability · https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01, ASI02; OWASP threat T6, T2

docs.title: RISK-049 · Escape from evaluation or sandbox containment onto live systems
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Roles and Access Controls (DSN-02) + Capability: Code Execution (CAP-10) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Infrastructure and network (HZ-03), Identity and access management (HZ-04), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when an agent that can execute code, operating in what is intended to be a contained setting — an evaluation, a red-team exercise, or a sandboxed task — reaches real systems because containment is incomplete: network egress is open, real credentials or accounts are present, or the objective can be pursued more easily outside the boundary. Capable agents have inferred that they were being evaluated and attacked third-party infrastructure to satisfy the task, and have taken unsanctioned actions against real people and organisations during cyber testing. As a result, activity meant to be harmless produces real-world security incidents.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0029 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Grant agents only the minimum permissions required for their designated tasks
  • CTRL-0040 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Limit the scope of agent actions through predefined thresholds and baselines
  • CTRL-0065 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Ensure every agent can be immediately paused or terminated by its operators
  • CTRL-0069 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Run agent-generated code only in isolated compute environments with network access blocked by default
  • CTRL-0089 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enforce default-deny network egress for agent runtimes, allowing only approved destinations
  • CTRL-0092 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Contain evaluations and red-team exercises so that agents cannot reach real systems, credentials, or people

Sources: https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026 · https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/ · https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/incident-report-unsanctioned-agent-behaviour-during-cyber-testing

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI10, ASI03; OWASP threat T13, T7

docs.title: RISK-051 · Unsanctioned coordination between agents
docs.text:
Arises from: Design: Agentic Architecture (DSN-01) + Capability: Agent Delegation (CAP-02) Failure mode: Agent Failure · Type: Safety, Security · Hazards: Identity and access management (HZ-04), Compromised user safety (HZ-08)

This risk arises when agents in a multi-agent system coordinate through channels or in ways that no operator sanctioned — sharing credentials, leaving each other messages in shared stores, using side channels, or dividing up a task so that each agent's actions look acceptable while the combined outcome is not. Coordination can emerge from shared objectives without any explicit instruction, and standard per-agent monitoring does not see it. As a result, the system as a whole pursues outcomes that would have been blocked had a single agent attempted them.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0024 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
  • CTRL-0026 (Level 1 · Standard): Require all agents to authenticate with verifiable, cryptographically signed identities before processing requests
  • CTRL-0028 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Continuously monitor multi-agent systems for cascade failure indicators
  • CTRL-0093 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Monitor agents for deceptive and collusive behaviour using an independent monitor
  • CTRL-0065 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Ensure every agent can be immediately paused or terminated by its operators

Sources: https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/incident-report-unsanctioned-agent-behaviour-during-cyber-testing · https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14143 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11369

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI10, ASI07; OWASP threat T13, T12

docs.title: RISK-055 · Data exfiltration through message and API channels
docs.text:
Arises from: Capability: Other Programmatic Interfaces (CAP-09) + Capability: File and Data Management (CAP-11) Failure mode: External Manipulation · Type: Security · Hazards: Data (HZ-01)

This risk arises when an agent that reads messages or data sent by outside parties through a programmatic channel — email, chat, support tickets, form submissions, webhooks, or API responses — also holds access to sensitive data and can send messages or make API calls outward. Instructions injected in an inbound message can then direct the agent to send data out through a legitimate channel: replying or forwarding to an attacker's address, posting to a shared channel, or calling an API with data in its parameters or in a URL. Unlike RISK-047, no web access is needed, because the message channel is both the way in and the way out. As a result, confidential data can leave the organisation without any single control being bypassed, as demonstrated by EchoLeak, where a single crafted email led Microsoft 365 Copilot to send internal data to an attacker, and ForcedLeak, where instructions in a web-form submission led Salesforce Agentforce to exfiltrate CRM records.

Controls:

  • CTRL-0020 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Use a dedicated LLM to extract required fields from inputs and filter out extraneous text or embedded instructions
  • CTRL-0062 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Implement input guardrails to detect prompt injection and adversarial attacks
  • CTRL-0082 (Level 2 · Best Practice): Do not grant agents access to personally identifiable or sensitive data unless strictly required
  • CTRL-0083 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Disallow unknown or external files unless they have been scanned for threats
  • CTRL-0089 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Enforce default-deny network egress for agent runtimes, allowing only approved destinations
  • CTRL-0090 (Level 1 · Standard): Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
  • CTRL-0097 (Level 0 · Cardinal): Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent

Sources: https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/uploads/2026/06/FMF-Issue-Brief-on-Emerging-Security-Practices-for-AI-Agents.pdf · https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ · https://www.hackthebox.com/blog/cve-2025-32711-echoleak-copilot-vulnerability · https://www.varonis.com/blog/forcedleak

Crosswalks: OWASP ASI ASI01, ASI02; OWASP threat T6, T2

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Level 0 controls are cardinal, Level 1 standard and Level 2 best practice; Controls → Control levels defines when each applies.

docs.title: CTRL-0001 · Use only LLMs from verified and trusted model developers
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-001

Untrusted or unknown model developers may introduce backdoors, data exfiltration risks, or inconsistent safety guarantees that compromise your agentic system. Establish evaluation criteria to assess model provider trustworthiness before adoption, including verification of published model cards, transparent responsible disclosure policies, evidence of security audits, and documented data handling practices. Evaluate whether the provider has an established track record, active security team, and clear incident response procedures. Regularly reassess providers against these criteria as new information emerges or the threat landscape evolves.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0002 · Obtain legally binding no-training and no-logging agreements from LLM API service providers
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-001

Without contractual protections, API providers may train models on your proprietary data or retain logs containing sensitive information, creating data leakage and compliance risks. Configure API settings to opt out of data logging and model training where available, and have your legal team review provider terms of service and data processing agreements to verify these protections are legally enforceable. Ensure alignment with your organisation's data governance and privacy requirements (e.g., GDPR, PDPA). Maintain records of these agreements and configurations for audit and compliance purposes.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1; IMDA MGF 2.2.1; OWASP ASI ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0003 · Use only established and verified model loaders in production environments
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-001

Malicious or unvetted model loaders may execute arbitrary code during model deserialisation, potentially introducing backdoors or system vulnerabilities. Use well-maintained, community-vetted model loading libraries with active security support and regular updates. Examples include Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, or official framework loaders (PyTorch, TensorFlow), whilst avoiding custom or unmaintained deserialisation code. Monitor for security advisories affecting your chosen loaders and apply patches promptly.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1; OWASP ASI ASI04, ASI05

docs.title: CTRL-0004 · Review the LLM's system card to inform risk assessment and model selection
docs.text:
Level 2 · Best Practice · Mitigates: RISK-002, RISK-003

System cards provide essential information about model capabilities, limitations, known failure modes, and safety evaluations that directly inform deployment decisions. Obtain and review the model's system card (or model card) before deployment, paying particular attention to documented risks, benchmark performance on safety evaluations, and limitations relevant to your use case. Use this information to identify potential misalignment between model behaviour and your application requirements, and to inform additional safeguards or testing strategies. If a system card is unavailable or incomplete, consider this a red flag when assessing provider trustworthiness.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1; IMDA MGF 2.1.1; OWASP ASI ASI10

docs.title: CTRL-0005 · Conduct structured evaluation of multiple LLMs for instruction-following, performance, and safety before deployment
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-002, RISK-003

Deploying an LLM without comparative evaluation risks selecting a model poorly suited to your use case, potentially resulting in safety issues, poor performance, or misaligned behaviour. Define evaluation criteria aligned with your application requirements (e.g., accuracy on domain-specific tasks, refusal of unsafe requests, consistency of outputs) and benchmark multiple candidate models against these criteria using representative test scenarios. Use both automated metrics and human evaluation to assess instruction-following quality, safety boundaries, and failure modes. Document evaluation results to support model selection decisions and establish baseline performance expectations for ongoing monitoring.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.2, 3.2; IMDA MGF 2.3.2; OWASP ASI ASI10

docs.title: CTRL-0006 · Require human approval before executing high-impact actions
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-001, RISK-002, RISK-003, RISK-019, RISK-020, RISK-052

Autonomous execution of high-impact actions without human oversight creates unacceptable risk of unintended consequences, including financial loss, data deletion, reputational damage, or safety incidents. Implement approval workflows that pause agent execution before critical actions (e.g., financial transactions, data deletion, external communications, system configuration changes) and present the proposed action with sufficient context for informed human decision-making. Design the approval interface to clearly display what will be executed, why the agent selected this action, and potential consequences. Ensure approval mechanisms cannot be bypassed by the agent and maintain audit logs of all approval decisions. Approval steps decay under volume: in one large deployment users approved about 93% of permission prompts. Pair this control with CTRL-0094 - measure approval and override rates, route routine actions to automated screening, and reserve human approval for genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions so that the approvals that remain are real decisions.

References: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.4; IMDA MGF 2.2.2; OWASP ASI ASI01, ASI09

docs.title: CTRL-0007 · Log all LLM inputs and outputs for regular review
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-001, RISK-002, RISK-003, RISK-050

Comprehensive logging enables post-incident analysis, safety monitoring, detection of adversarial inputs, and continuous improvement of LLM behaviour over time. Implement structured logging that captures all LLM inputs, outputs, timestamps, model versions, and relevant metadata (user ID, session ID, tool calls). Use a centralised logging system (e.g., ELK stack, Datadog, CloudWatch) with appropriate retention policies and access controls to protect sensitive data. Establish regular review processes—manual spot-checks or automated anomaly detection—to identify drift, unsafe outputs, or emerging failure patterns.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.3; OWASP ASI ASI08

docs.title: CTRL-0008 · Implement automated alerts when agent behaviour drifts from predefined thresholds
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-002, RISK-022

Behavioural drift may indicate model degradation, adversarial manipulation, or emergent unsafe patterns that require immediate investigation. Define baseline metrics for expected agent behaviour (e.g., tool usage patterns, response times, error rates, decision distributions) and establish acceptable variance thresholds based on your risk tolerance. Implement monitoring systems that continuously track these metrics and trigger alerts when deviations exceed thresholds, enabling rapid response to anomalies. Configure alerts to include sufficient diagnostic context (timestamp, affected sessions, deviation magnitude) and establish clear escalation procedures for investigating and remediating drift incidents.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.3; OWASP ASI ASI10

docs.title: CTRL-0009 · Use only tool servers and APIs, including MCP servers, that implement robust authentication mechanisms in production environments
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-004, RISK-054

Weak or misconfigured authorisation on the servers and APIs that an agent's tools call can lead to unauthorised access, token theft, or privilege escalation that compromises connected systems. Before deployment, verify that every remote tool endpoint authenticates its caller with a standard mechanism (for example OAuth 2.1, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, or mutually authenticated TLS) and enforces per-client scopes, and reject endpoints that rely on hard-coded credentials, unscoped shared keys, or deprecated authentication methods; test the authorisation flows in a development environment to confirm them. For MCP servers, also verify per-client consent flows and redirect URI validation to prevent authorisation bypasses, and reject servers with insufficient session management. As of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, verify additionally that the server implements RFC 9207 issuer identification (so a client can detect a substituted authorization server) and Client ID Metadata Documents in place of dynamic client registration, and prefer servers that support the Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension so that access is governed by your identity provider rather than by per-user ad-hoc consent. Treat servers still built on the pre-2026 stateful session model as needing review before production use.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices · https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1, 3.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI03, ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0010 · Use only MCP servers that validate credentials on every inbound request
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-004

Relying on session state or connection-based authentication without per-request validation creates vulnerability to session hijacking, token replay attacks, and unauthorised access after initial authentication. Verify that MCP servers implement stateless authentication by validating credentials (e.g., OAuth tokens, API keys) on every single request rather than caching authorisation decisions based on connection or session state. Test this behaviour by monitoring whether the server accepts requests with expired, revoked, or missing credentials after an initial successful authentication. Ensure the server responds with appropriate HTTP 401 errors when credentials are invalid, expired, or absent, forcing re-authentication rather than relying on stale authorisation state. The 2026-07-28 specification removes long-lived stateful sessions from the protocol core, making per-request validation the expected behaviour; treat a server whose authorization depends on session state as non-compliant.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices · https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.6; IMDA MGF 2.1.2; OWASP ASI ASI03

docs.title: CTRL-0011 · Limit token scopes to the minimum privileges required and avoid broad or wildcard scopes
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-005

Overly broad token scopes enable compromised or malicious actors to access resources beyond what is necessary for legitimate operations, amplifying the impact of security breaches. Define granular, task-specific scopes for each MCP server integration and request only the minimum permissions required for the intended functionality (e.g., "read:inventory" rather than "admin:*"). Review and document the justification for each requested scope during integration, and reject MCP servers that require unnecessarily broad permissions or fail to support fine-grained scope definitions. Periodically audit active token scopes to identify and revoke excessive permissions that may have accumulated over time.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.6, 2.8; IMDA MGF 2.1.2; OWASP ASI ASI03

docs.title: CTRL-0012 · Use only MCP servers that integrate with authorisation servers implementing per-client consent mechanisms
docs.text:
Level 2 · Best Practice · Mitigates: RISK-005

Without explicit per-client consent, a malicious or compromised client could abuse delegated permissions to access resources the user never intended to authorise for that specific application. Verify that MCP servers integrate with OAuth 2.1 authorisation servers that implement per-client consent flows, where users explicitly approve each client-permission combination rather than granting blanket permissions across all clients. The authorisation server should clearly identify the requesting client and display what data or actions are being requested during the consent flow. Ensure the authorisation server persists consent decisions and provides mechanisms for users to review and revoke previously granted permissions. With Client ID Metadata Documents (2026-07-28 specification), the authorization server identifies the client from its published metadata; check that consent screens name the client accurately, and use the Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension where a central identity provider should govern access on behalf of all users.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/authorization · https://aaronparecki.com/2025/11/25/1/mcp-authorization-spec-update · https://stytch.com/blog/mcp-authentication-and-authorization-servers/ · https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 3.3; IMDA MGF 2.1.2; OWASP ASI ASI03

docs.title: CTRL-0013 · Test all untested MCP servers in a sandboxed environment before deploying to production
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-006, RISK-048

Untested MCP servers may contain vulnerabilities, malicious code, or unexpected behaviours that could compromise your production systems or data. Deploy MCP servers first to an isolated sandbox environment (e.g., containerised test environment, separate network segment, or dedicated development infrastructure) to evaluate their security posture, behaviour, and reliability. Monitor server activity during testing for anomalous network connections, excessive resource consumption, unauthorised file access, or other suspicious behaviours. Only promote MCP servers to production after successful security review, functional testing, and verification that the server behaves as documented.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.9; IMDA MGF 2.3.2; OWASP ASI ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0014 · Use only MCP servers from verified and trusted developers
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-006, RISK-048

Untrusted or unknown MCP server developers may introduce malicious functionality, security vulnerabilities, or data exfiltration mechanisms that compromise your agentic system. Establish evaluation criteria to assess MCP server developer trustworthiness before adoption, including verification of public code repositories, community reputation, security disclosure practices, and maintenance history. Evaluate whether the developer has a track record of responding to security issues, maintains active development, and provides transparent documentation of server capabilities. Prioritise MCP servers from the official Model Context Protocol repository, well-established organisations, or developers with verified identities and demonstrated security practices.

References: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.1, 3.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0015 · Treat all tool metadata and outputs as untrusted input requiring validation
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-006, RISK-007, RISK-048

Tool metadata (descriptions, parameter names, schema definitions) can contain prompt injection attacks that manipulate agent behaviour even without tool invocation, whilst tool outputs may contain malicious content designed to compromise downstream systems. Validate and sanitise all tool metadata before exposing it to the LLM, treating tool descriptions with the same scrutiny as external user input and implementing content filtering to detect embedded instructions or adversarial prompts. Apply strict schema validation to tool outputs and sanitise responses before using them in prompts, displaying them to users, or passing them to other systems. Implement monitoring and logging of tool metadata and outputs to enable detection of injection attempts and post-incident analysis of compromised tool behaviour.

References: https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/model-context-protocol-security-risks-and-exploits/ · https://simonwillison.net/2025/Apr/9/mcp-prompt-injection/ · https://www.practical-devsecops.com/mcp-security-vulnerabilities/

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.1, 3.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI02, ASI04

docs.title: CTRL-0016 · Define clearly the agent's role, scope, and non-goals in the system prompt
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-008

Ambiguous or missing role definitions allow agents to interpret requests too broadly, potentially executing actions outside intended boundaries or misunderstanding their authority and constraints. Explicitly define the agent's purpose, permitted actions, and operational boundaries in the system prompt, including clear statements about what the agent should not do or attempt. Document specific examples of in-scope and out-of-scope behaviours to reduce ambiguity and guide the agent's decision-making in edge cases. Regularly review and refine these definitions based on observed agent behaviour, ensuring role boundaries remain aligned with evolving use cases and risk tolerances.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.3; IMDA MGF 2.1.2; OWASP ASI ASI01

docs.title: CTRL-0017 · Define clear success criteria for the agent's tasks
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-008

Without explicit success criteria, agents may pursue task completion using inappropriate methods, over-optimise for partial objectives, or fail to recognise when they have achieved the intended outcome. Define measurable, verifiable success criteria for each task or category of tasks the agent performs, specifying both what constitutes successful completion and acceptable quality standards. Include criteria that address not just functional outcomes but also safety constraints, resource limits, and acceptable trade-offs. Regularly evaluate whether the agent's interpretation of success criteria aligns with intended outcomes and refine definitions to address observed gaps or misalignments.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.3, 3.2; IMDA MGF 2.1.2; OWASP ASI ASI01

docs.title: CTRL-0018 · Define default behaviour when the agent encounters ambiguous situations
docs.text:
Level 2 · Best Practice · Mitigates: RISK-008

Agents encountering ambiguous instructions without clear fallback behaviour may make incorrect assumptions, proceed with risky actions, or halt unexpectedly, reducing reliability and increasing safety risks. Establish a default policy for handling ambiguity that aligns with your risk tolerance, such as requesting human clarification, selecting the most conservative option, or declining to act until uncertainty is resolved. Document this policy in the system prompt and provide examples of ambiguous scenarios to guide agent decision-making. Monitor how often the agent invokes ambiguity handling mechanisms to identify areas where task definitions or instructions require clarification.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.10; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI01

docs.title: CTRL-0019 · Keep untrusted inputs out of system instructions, and enclose any untrusted content given to the model in delimiters marked as data
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-009

Prompt injection attacks exploit LLMs' inability to distinguish between instructions and data, allowing malicious users to embed commands within input that override intended behaviour. Do not interpolate user input, retrieved content, or tool outputs into the system prompt or other instruction templates; fix the system prompt at build time and pass untrusted content to the model in the user or tool turns, where it carries less authority. Where untrusted content must be quoted, enclose it within clearly marked boundaries (e.g., XML tags or special markers) that are unlikely to appear naturally in the input, and instruct the LLM to treat delimited content as data rather than instructions. Neither measure is a complete defence, because the model can still follow instructions in untrusted content, so combine them with controls that do not depend on the model's compliance, such as a deterministic policy layer (CTRL-0090) and least privilege (CTRL-0029).

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.1; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI01

docs.title: CTRL-0020 · Use a dedicated LLM to extract required fields from inputs and filter out extraneous text or embedded instructions
docs.text:
Level 2 · Best Practice · Mitigates: RISK-009, RISK-047, RISK-055

Using the same LLM for both input processing and task execution creates vulnerability to prompt injection attacks embedded in user input. Deploy a separate LLM instance configured specifically for input sanitisation, with explicit instructions to extract only designated fields (e.g., name, email, query text) whilst ignoring any other content including embedded commands or meta-instructions. Configure this extraction LLM with a restrictive system prompt focused solely on structured data extraction and validation against expected schemas. Validate extracted fields against expected formats before passing them to the main agent LLM, and monitor extraction outputs for anomalies that might indicate injection attempts.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.1, 2.9; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI01

docs.title: CTRL-0021 · Implement allowlists and denylists to restrict what categories of information can be written to the agent's persistent memory
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-010, RISK-011

Unrestricted writes to persistent memory enable attackers to poison agent memory with malicious instructions, false information, or sensitive data that could compromise future agent behaviour or leak confidential information. Define explicit allowlists of permitted memory categories (e.g., user preferences, conversation context, task history) and denylists of forbidden content (e.g., credentials, system instructions, security policies, prompt overrides). Enforce these restrictions at the memory write interface, validating all write operations against the defined policies before persisting data.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.6, 2.7; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI06

docs.title: CTRL-0022 · Implement content filtering on writes to persistent memory to detect and block known unsafe content patterns
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-010

Malicious actors may attempt to inject adversarial content into agent memory that bypasses category-based restrictions, such as jailbreak prompts, command injection templates, or social engineering content designed to manipulate future agent behaviour. Deploy content filtering mechanisms that scan all memory write operations for known unsafe patterns (e.g., jailbreak strings, tool invocation templates, prompt override attempts, phishing content) before persisting data. Implement filtering using prompt injection detectors (to detect jailbreak strings) or custom classifiers finetuned on specific risks (e.g. attempts to invoke tools maliciously).

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.1; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI06

docs.title: CTRL-0023 · Log all modifications to persistent memory with comprehensive source metadata for audit purposes
docs.text:
Level 2 · Best Practice · Mitigates: RISK-010, RISK-011

Without detailed audit logs, detecting and investigating memory poisoning attacks becomes extremely difficult, preventing effective incident response and forensic analysis. Implement comprehensive logging for all memory write, update, and delete operations, capturing source metadata including timestamps, user or agent identity, session context, and the specific content being modified. Structure logs to enable correlation analysis, allowing security teams to trace how specific memory entries evolved over time and identify suspicious modification patterns. Store audit logs in a tamper-evident system separate from the agent's operational memory to prevent attackers from covering their tracks by deleting or modifying log entries.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 4.3; IMDA MGF 2.3.3; OWASP ASI ASI06, ASI08

docs.title: CTRL-0024 · Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
docs.text:
Level 0 · Cardinal · Mitigates: RISK-012, RISK-022, RISK-051, RISK-053

Unstructured or inadequately validated inter-agent messages create vulnerability to injection attacks, misinterpretation, and parsing errors that could compromise agent behaviour or cascade through multi-agent systems. Define explicit message schemas using formal specification languages (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that specify required fields, data types, validation rules, and permitted value ranges for all agent-to-agent communications. Implement strict input validation that verifies all incoming messages conform to expected schemas, checking field presence, data types, value ranges, and structural integrity before processing message content. Reject messages that are incomplete, contain unexpected fields, violate type constraints, or include suspicious patterns, returning explicit error responses to the sending agent and logging validation failures to enable detection of compromised or malfunctioning agents.

Crosswalks: CSA Addendum 2.7, 3.4; IMDA MGF 2.3.1; OWASP ASI ASI07

docs.title: CTRL-0025 · Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
docs.text:
Level 1 · Standard · Mitigates: RISK-012, RISK-022, RISK-053

Unencrypted inter-agent communications expose sensitive data, credentials, and operational context to network-based attackers through eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks.
